prohibited_recommendations: Do not give IV thrombolysis before non-contrast CT excludes intracranial haemorrhage.
Do not give IV thrombolysis while blood pressure is 185/110 mmHg or higher.
Do not give IV thrombolysis if INR is above 1.7, the platelet count is below 100,000, there was recent major surgery, or another guideline-listed contraindication is present.
Do not delay non-contrast CT for additional imaging or laboratory results in a stroke alert.
Do not delay thrombectomy to observe the response to IV thrombolysis.
Do not start anticoagulation within 24 hours of IV thrombolysis or before follow-up imaging excludes haemorrhagic transformation, and do not bridge with heparin.
Do not discharge on aspirin alone for atrial fibrillation-related cardioembolic stroke.
required_recommendations: Establish last known well (09:00, 2 hours 22 minutes before arrival) and the NIHSS (16).

IV thrombolysis: give once blood pressure is below 185/110 mmHg (2 hours 22 minutes from last known well; warfarin stopped 4 months ago, INR 1.1; platelets 179; glucose 240 mg/dL is not a contraindication). Thrombectomy: proceed for the distal left M1 occlusion extending into the superior M2 division (NIHSS 16, living independently before the stroke, ASPECTS 10, within 6 hours); do not wait for the response to thrombolysis.
Achieve a door-to-needle time under 60 minutes.

Lower blood pressure below 185/110 mmHg (206/105 on arrival) with IV labetalol or nicardipine before IV thrombolysis, then keep it below 180/105 mmHg for 24 hours; after successful recanalization do not target systolic blood pressure below 140 mmHg.

Proceed with CTA without waiting for creatinine; a prior mild contrast reaction and CKD stage 3a do not justify delaying vessel imaging. Give premedication only if it causes no delay, and have treatment for a reaction at hand.
Treat hyperglycaemia (glucose 240 mg/dL) to 140 to 180 mg/dL during the first 24 hours, avoiding hypoglycaemia with her glipizide and insulin.
Admit to a stroke unit with continuous cardiac monitoring (telemetry) for at least the first 24 hours.
Control the ventricular rate of atrial fibrillation (106 to 114 bpm on arrival; she takes no rate-control medicine) with a beta-blocker, avoiding hypotension.

Repeat troponin and review the ECG; the mild elevation (troponin I 0.05 ng/mL) is most likely demand ischaemia from rapid atrial fibrillation or neurogenic myocardial injury; it does not delay reperfusion.
Recheck sodium (129 mEq/L), give isotonic fluids only, and assess volume status in view of her heart failure and furosemide.

Start apixaban 5 mg twice daily for atrial fibrillation (CHA2DS2-VASc 7; HAS-BLED 4 for uncontrolled hypertension, this stroke, age over 65 and aspirin) on day 6 to 7 for this major infarct (more than one cortical MCA branch), once follow-up imaging excludes haemorrhagic transformation; do not bridge with heparin, and stop aspirin when apixaban starts.
Address her reasons for stopping warfarin (bruising, fear of bleeding after a fall): bruising is not a contraindication, and a DOAC carries a lower intracranial bleeding risk than warfarin.
Intensify lipid lowering (LDL 118 mg/dL on rosuvastatin 20 mg) to an LDL below 70 mg/dL, with rosuvastatin 40 mg or added ezetimibe, for carotid atherosclerosis and diabetes.

Blood pressure 206/105 must be lowered below 185/110 mmHg before thrombolysis; elevated pressure in acute stroke is not by itself a hypertensive haemorrhage or PRES.

NIHSS 16 (LOC questions 2, gaze 1, visual 1, face 1, right arm 3, right leg 3, sensory 1, language 2, extinction 2) with a distal left M1 occlusion: thrombectomy is indicated within 6 hours (AHA/ASA 2026, COR 1), with IV thrombolysis first.
Expressive aphasia with right face and arm weakness in a left-handed woman localises to the left MCA superior division; most left-handed people are left-hemisphere dominant for language.
A normal non-contrast CT under 3 hours does not exclude infarction; the MRI shows DWI restriction without FLAIR change, as expected in the hyperacute window.
A prior mild contrast reaction and CKD stage 3a do not justify delaying CTA in a thrombectomy candidate.
Atrial fibrillation off anticoagulation with heart failure, hypertension, diabetes and female sex (CHA2DS2-VASc 7) is the mechanism (TOAST cardioembolism); carotid plaque is under 50%.

AHA/ASA 2026 sequencing: glucose is checked before thrombolysis, but routine CBC/coagulation results are not awaited without a reason to expect abnormality; ECG/troponin do not delay reperfusion, and CTA/CTP do not wait for creatinine.

patient.history_present_illness: Mrs. Doreen Caldwell is a 68-year-old left-handed African American woman with a history of atrial fibrillation (self-discontinued warfarin 4 months ago), poorly controlled hypertension, type 2 diabetes on insulin and oral agents, HFpEF, and CKD stage 3a, who was brought by ambulance to the emergency department after her daughter called 911 when she arrived for a scheduled visit and found her mother on the living room floor. The daughter reports speaking to her mother by phone at approximately 09:00 this morning, at which time she sounded entirely normal. The daughter arrived at the home at 10:45 and found the front door unlocked. She discovered her mother sitting on the floor next to the couch, leaning against it, with her right arm limp at her side. Mrs. Caldwell was attempting to speak but her words were garbled and she appeared confused and frightened. There was no evidence of head trauma, urinary incontinence, or tongue biting. No vomiting was reported. EMS arrived at 10:58 and documented right-sided hemiparesis with facial droop and expressive aphasia. A prehospital stroke alert was activated. Prehospital fingerstick glucose was 202 mg/dL. The cardiac monitor showed an irregularly irregular rhythm without distinct P waves, consistent with atrial fibrillation. She was transported to our comprehensive stroke center with arrival at 11:22. On ED assessment, Mrs. Caldwell was alert but distressed, speaking in short effortful phrases. She was able to state her name but could not reliably provide her birthdate or describe what happened. Her daughter confirmed that the last known well time was 09:00, approximately 2 hours and 22 minutes before ED arrival. Her daughter also confirmed that Mrs. Caldwell stopped taking warfarin approximately four months ago because she was developing large bruises on her arms and was worried about falling and bleeding.
